NPR News
This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
NPR |
By
Ron Elving
Published October 24, 2026 at 2:00 AM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Saul Loeb
AFP via Getty Images
New speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., holds the gavel during the opening session of the 116th Congress at the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 3, 2019.
Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.
But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.
That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
Sponsored
These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.
Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.
But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.
The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.
All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.
Flexing midterm muscles
Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.
Sponsored
It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.
That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.
If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.
That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.
National Archives /
The "Democratic New Year's Eve Cheer" cartoon from Dec. 31, 1931, reflects the Democrats' win of the House that year after special elections.
The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.
After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.
Pendulum swings both ways
Sponsored
Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years ( below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.
Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.
In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate.
The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.
What goes up …
AFP via Getty Images / AFP
Demonstrators carrying signs against the war in Vietnam march in front of the White House in April 1965 in Washington, D.C.
But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.
Sponsored

Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
NPR |
By
The Associated Press
Published October 24, 2026 at 12:04 AM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Abdulnasser Alseddik
AP
FILE - Smoke rises after an attack by Houthi rebels on the city of Taiz, Yemen, on Oct. 21, 2015. (AP Photo/Abdulnasser Alseddik, File)
Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.
The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.
Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.
Sponsored
"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.
Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.
The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.
Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."
Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells
Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.
War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.
Sponsored
By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.
As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.
The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food
Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.
Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.
Sponsored
Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.
These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.
"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.
Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.
Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.
"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.
Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

Washington school safety experts talk about mission, funding, challenges
KUOW |
By
Kim Malcolm,
John O'Brien
Published October 23, 2026 at 6:05 PM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Flickr Photo/Larry Darling
School buses are lined up outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place, on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Bend, Oregon.
In the wake of last week’s mass shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, KUOW’s All Things Considered asked about efforts to keep Washington state schools safe, including physical safety measures on school campuses, how threats are assessed and prevented, and funding for those efforts. The Washington approach is layered, and there are no simple answers.
Jessica Vavrus, the executive director of the Washington Association of Educational Service Districts, said the state has funded three key roles in each of the nine districts.
“One is related to behavioral health navigation, so that's just resource identification and support within communities broadly around safety and behavioral health, mental health services,” she said. “The second is threat assessment, and the third is comprehensive safety. That involves following and maintaining supports around all the requirements related to school safety, navigating that morass of state requirements that schools have from the Legislature to make sure, ultimately, that students are safe but also that school districts are meeting their expectations under the law.”
Sponsored
Crime
Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school before being killed by witness
Associated Press
Vavrus told KUOW Washington reported just over 1,100 threat assessments statewide last year.
Jason McPherson, a threat assessment coordinator at Educational Service District 101 in Spokane, said funding is always an issue as is aging infrastructure.
“Even if a building's five years old, the threats that we experienced five years ago are going to be different than what we see today,” McPherson said. “We hope that they continue to receive additional funding in the future to address safety concerns within their buildings.”
McPherson said threat assessment coordinators like him wear many hats. Their main goal is to partner with school districts to implement Washington’s chosen threat assessment model, the Salem-Keizer Cascade model. Originally developed in Oregon, that approach involves collaborative, evidence-based threat assessments designed to prevent school violence through early intervention. Washington state adopted it in 2019.
The model includes both public school districts and private schools that may want to partner with them, plus community agencies that work with children.
“The important part is that they're trained to look for behaviors that indicate that students are moving along a pathway to violence, towards targeted violence,” McPherson said. “It's really not that they're making threats, but their behaviors indicate that they may be moving along a pathway to violence. And the goal is to identify interventions that will help that student remain in the school and be a safe member of the school community.”
“We want teachers to feel safe being at school. We want kids to feel safe being at school. We want parents to feel safe sending their kids to school, but how are we going to do that?” he added. “That usually includes both interventions for the student and creating safety plans to ensure that everybody at the school is safe.”
Sponsored
Crime
Examining Washington school safety after shooting in Bend
Kim Malcolm, John O'Brien
Marissa Rathbone is the assistant executive director of government relations at the Washington Association of School Administrators, which helps school districts implement state policies in their buildings and classrooms.
“Our public education system is chronically underfunded for basic education,” she said. “There's something called a prototypical school funding model. That's basically a formula that allocates a portion of an FTE (Full-Time Equivalent) based on the number of students in the district. It hasn't been updated for many, many years. It hasn't been updated to respond to some of these evolving or changing needs for school safety, whether we're talking about counselors, psychologists, or other school safety staff.”
Rathbone said that chronic underfunding makes it difficult for school districts to meet all of their communities’ needs.
“The message I really want to leave you with is that school districts care deeply about ensuring that students have a sense of belonging, that they're coming to school feeling safe, that staff are doing the same,” she said. “One of the solutions I would propose is that the Legislature fulfills their requirements of basic education by ensuring that they're funding for the basic education requirements and updating the prototypical school funding model, so the staffing allocations are updated for today's school district needs and building needs, including to ensure that there are enough staff to ensure the safety of our students.”

By
Ava Berger
Published October 23, 2026 at 5:40 PM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
South Fork Fire Rescue
AP
Floodwaters surround trailers at the Fun Valley Family Resort campground and RV part in South Fork, Colo., early Friday, Oct. 23, 2026.
Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."
Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.
"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."
Sponsored
Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.
"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."
Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.
Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.
Thick, brown floodwaters
Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.
In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."
Sponsored
We are closely monitoring the flash flooding in Hurricane. Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted.
Please follow all evacuation orders and local emergency guidance. We’re grateful to the first responders working to keep Utahns safe. https://t.co/8hDQ85T0Xz— Governor Cox (@GovCox) October 22, 2026
The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.
In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."
"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.
The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.
The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.
The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.
Sponsored
A record amount of rainfall
The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.
Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.
Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.
"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.
While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.
The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.
Sponsored
Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

KUOW |
By
Ruby de Luna
Published October 23, 2026 at 5:07 PM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Photo courtesy of Aigen
Aigen's solar-powered robot weeder known as Element Gen 2 works its way through a field picking out weeds with its four metal arms.
A Redmond-based startup has developed a solar-powered weeder using AI technology to help distinguish weed from crop.
The weeder, known as the Element Gen 2, looks like a drafting table on wheels. The top surface is a solar panel that powers the machine. Underneath it are four metal arms that pluck the weeds and fling them behind it as it rolls through a farm plot.
Richard Wurden, cofounder of Aigen, the company behind the weeder, said the conventional method for weeding low-cost crops often involves spraying herbicides.
Sponsored
“We wanted to figure out how do we do that without diesel, and to do that without spraying chemicals,” Wurden said.
That’s significant because one of the challenges in weed control is that weeds are adaptable.
Rui Liu, assistant professor of weed science at Washington State University, said repeated use of herbicides can lead to resistant strains of weeds, making the chemicals ineffective.
“As a result, growers need diverse management strategies to maintain long- term weed control,” Liu said.
For Aigen founders, the pursuit of non-toxic weed control was personal. Wurden has Type 1 diabetes. Co-founder Kenny Lee has non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Both diseases have been linked to pesticide use.
Aigen isn’t the only start-up to develop technology for farming.
Seattle-based Carbon Robotics uses AI detection and laser weeding technology. But many companies still rely on diesel to power their equipment.
Sponsored
“That’s why we took the most efficient possible approach where you don’t need to refill something,” Wurden said. “When somebody goes and refills it and brings a truck out there, is it really autonomous? Solar is actually autonomous.”
With rising fuel prices, Wurden said they’ve received more than 30 orders for their solar-powered models.

KUOW |
By
Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard
Published October 23, 2026 at 5:00 PM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
AP Photo/Ted S. Warren, File
A person puts their ballot in a drop box on Oct. 27, 2020, at a library in Seattle.
It’s unclear what role federal election monitors will play or how many there will be in King County on Election Day.
The U.S. Department of Justice informed King County Elections Director Julie Wise this week that the administration is sending election monitors for the Nov. 3 midterms.
“As the Civil Rights Division has done in the past, our monitors only observe,” the Justice Department’s Anelise Powers wrote in an email to Wise. “They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process.”
Sponsored
Unlike other states with polling places, Washington has long voted by mail, a system that has faced allegations and legal threats from President Donald Trump. Voting commenced last week ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Voters can vote in person at their county election center, but almost all ballots are returned via drop box or the mail.
The monitors will look for compliance with federal voting rights and disability access laws. The Trump administration has also used voting laws, including the National Voter Registration Act and Help America Vote Act, as legal backing in its push for the state’s sensitive voter data, one of several flashpoints between the state and federal government over elections this year. A judge tossed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking this data.
Trump has repeatedly espoused claims of rampant fraud, and critics fear the monitors could use those false allegations to interfere in elections, which are run by states.
The Department of Justice described the actions it’ll take in Washington’s most populous county and elsewhere as “routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.”
“All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process,” spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in an email Friday. “Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
But Halei Watkins, spokesperson for King County Elections, said in her seven-plus years there, the county has “never been sent a monitor from the Department of Justice.”
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs’s office said the Department of Justice has sent elections observers to Washington in the past.
Sponsored
“We’re unaware of any issues stemming from their presence,” spokesperson Stefanie Randolph said in an email.
All observers — private citizens, or those affiliated with political parties and government agencies — have to abide by state law, she said.
“They may not touch ballots, voting equipment, tabulation machines or interfere with voting,” Randolph added. “County auditors have the authority to remove anyone who does not follow these rules from the premises.”
Washington is one of at least 10 states where it’s been reported that a county received a similar notification. Oregon’s Multnomah County, which covers Portland, is another. Pels said the Justice Department will have monitors in every state.
Monitors were also deployed during this year’s primary elections, with few reported issues. In Wyoming, however, Republican Gov. Mark Gordon was concerned the monitors were “aggressive” and “irregular.” Justice Department officials contested Gordon’s characterization.
Harmeet Dhillon, head of the federal agency’s Civil Rights Division, said last month that Department of Justice planned to send 1,000 monitors nationwide, which she called the “largest monitoring effort” ever.
In 2022, the department under then-President Joe Biden sent monitors to 64 locales in 24 states for those midterms, but none to Washington.

Need a Halloween boo-st? 8 last-minute ways to get spooky in Seattle
KUOW |
By
Cornelius Hocker
Published October 23, 2026 at 3:58 PM PDT
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Quilia via Unsplash
For fans of all things spooky, this Halloween season has been full of delightful frights.
New life has been given to classic horror films “ Carrie” and “ Friday the 13th” in the form of deep-dive, reimagined streaming series. Capitalizing on the success of the movie reboot, “ Halloween” now has an official video game that lets people either stalk as or be stalked by Michael Myers.
However, if jump scares on a television screen aren’t cutting it, there are plenty of options over the next two weekends for Seattleites to experience a real-life thrill or just to chill in your costume.
Sponsored
Haunted houses
Georgetown Morgue: Housed in what once served as an actual morgue and funeral home over several decades, the Georgetown Morgue offers those who dare to enter a frightening experience that changes each year. Through dimly light passageways, visitors traverse different rooms that are specifically made to titillate the senses. If you survive the haunted house, there’s also a dark maze right next door, but fair warning, you could get wet.
Price: $38 for general admission.
Open: Oct. 23-25; Oct. 28-Nov.1; and Nov. 5-7.
Nightfall Orphanage: If you want to get scared and give to charity, Nightfall is an option. Billed as a “high-end neighborhood home-haunt in West Seattle for the local community that raises donations for community-based charities,” its website dives into the deep fantasy lore surrounding Nightfall. The literature prepares brave souls for what they’re about to see.
Price: $20 per person with a food donation from your group or $25 per person in your group.
Open: Oct. 23-24 and Oct. 30-31.
Stalker Farm: Ever wanted to be dropped into a horror movie? That’s what Stalker Farm promises. Within rows and rows of corn paths for you to walk through, the haunts are full of creepy scenes that have been known to make some people cry and others laugh.
Price: $37.95 for two haunts and a corn maze.
Open: Oct. 23-24 and Oct. 30-Nov. 1.
Arts & Life
Seattle's got hex appeal. How local witches are cultivating the city's magic
Patricia Murphy, Caroline Chamberlain Gomez
Parties and performances
Boo Seattle: Taking place at the WAMU Theater, Boo Seattle promises three massive themed stages, more than 50 DJs, and performers over two nights, along with endless frights and surprises behind every door.
Sponsored
Price: General admission is $191.99 on Friday and $204.99 on Saturday.
Open: Oct. 30-31.
Dracula: Presented by the International Ballet Theatre, Bram Stroker’s Gothic tale is brought to life in a “performance blending theatre, modern dance, tap dance, gypsy dance, and ballet, with elaborate costumes and dark humor.”
Price: $91.60 - $181.60.
Open: Oct. 25.
Haunted Soiree: For fans of Oktoberfest, Halloween celebrations and true crime, Haunted Soiree blends all three. Described as an immersive cocktail party, guests will spend two hours roaming the halls of the 100-year-old Rainier Chapter House, teeming with spirits and mysteries.
Price: $70.25 - $78.25.
Open: Oct. 23-25 and Oct. 28-31.
This Is Halloween: A familiar character is going to do something unfamiliar in this parody following Jack Skellington from Tim Burton’s 1993 film “The Nightmare Before Christmas”. Bored of his usual terrifying antics and the monotony of Halloween Town, the Pumpkin King takes a fateful stroll through an enchanted forest that changes everything.
Price: $49, $55, or $64 depending on the night.
Open: Oct. 23-25 and Oct. 27-31.
Sponsored
Washington State Horror Con: As the Pacific Northwest’s largest celebrity horror convention, the three-day fan experience is dedicated to letting fans immerse themselves in all things spooky. You’ll get to meet some of the actors who’ve portrayed beloved characters from some of the most well-known horror genre movies and series, including “Candyman,” “The Walking Dead,” and “Saw.”
Price: $100 for a 3-day pass. $35 on Friday; $55 on Saturday; and $45 on Sunday.
Open: Oct. 23-25.
